title: Nature: Any Future Without It?
description: Ecology, and the last module of the book: the threats to the environment the course asks you to name, from ozone depletion, acid rain and water scarcity to deforestation, garbage dumping and the extinction of species, sorted into the natural disasters that happen whether or not anybody is there and the man-made ones that exist because of what people do; the five definitions of the module — a drought as a long period of dry weather, a flood as an overflowing of water over land, a tsunami as an unusually large sea wave from a seaquake or an undersea eruption, an earthquake as vibrations in the crust rated on the Richter scale, and a volcano as the vent through which lava, steam and ash are expelled — with the fact that a tsunami loses speed in shallower water while its height grows, the volcano dormant for a hundred and twenty-three years, and the motto of a campaign poster; the listening account of a mother whose daughter and son-in-law were caught by the tsunami of December 2004, in four parts, from the wedding and the honeymoon postponed until Christmas to the fund set up for the children the disaster orphaned, with the words of the passage, postpone, glimpse, turmoil, mourn, grief, dreadful, orphaned, livelihood, and the formulas for expressing sympathy; must and the perfect infinitive — deduction in the past, the difference between a conclusion about now and a conclusion about earlier, the obligation carried by had to instead, the negative conclusion carried by can't have, and the trap of the ordinary verb in must have something done; the study-based text on global warming, the clear evidence of human-produced warming in the oceans, the uncertainty it removes, the economic reason world leaders close their ears to it, the Kyoto Treaty, the accelerated glacier melting and the millions left without adequate summertime water, with the six synonyms of the exercise, impact, uncertainty, findings, implications, adequate and accelerated; will against be going to, with the four uses of each — a habitual action, a promise, an offer and something expected against a prior plan, a prediction read off present evidence, commands and refusals, and a permanent state — and the two questions that sort them, when the decision was taken and where the prediction comes from; the how-green-are-you quiz, the tap, the light bulb and the standby, and the three columns of reacting, from mild surprise through disbelief to shock and dismay; the two survivors' accounts of the writing section, the vocabulary of a disaster, from engulf, sweep and disintegrate to loot, perish, pin and grasp, the three past tenses of a narrative, including the past perfect passive, and the link between a cause and an effect carried by a conjunction, a preposition, a connector or a verb, with the swap between because and so and the opposite directions of result in and result from; and rhythm and intonation, the beat that falls on the words carrying the meaning, the sense groups that punctuation marks out, and the tones that close a statement, a WH question, a yes/no question and a list
